#163305. The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1361 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in the 17th century, Danish King Frederik III already knew that the legendary unicorn horn came from a real animal.
  • In a recent development, the narwhal's tusk is unlike almost any other tooth in nature.
  • This unusual biological structure caught the attention of an international team of researchers from several scientific disciplines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the 17th century, Danish King Frederik III already knew that the legendary unicorn horn came from a real animal. However, this creature had fins instead of hooves and inhabited the icy waters of the Arctic. The king dispatched an expedition to Greenland to investigate the source of these highly prized objects. The successful mission earned him a throne fashioned entirely from "unicorn horns," enhancing his power and prestige across Europe. Yet the treasured horn was not actually a horn, but "merely" a tooth.

In a recent development, the narwhal's tusk is unlike almost any other tooth in nature. Whereas elongated teeth, including elephant and walrus tusks and beaver incisors, grow in curved shapes, the male narwhal develops a remarkable corkscrew-shaped tooth. Typically, the upper left canine grows forward through the upper lip, twisting counterclockwise as it extends. It can reach two meters (6.6 feet) in length, equivalent to as much as half the animal's body length.

This unusual biological structure caught the attention of an international team of researchers from several scientific disciplines. Using advanced X-ray imaging techniques, they set out to determine whether the arrangement of the tusk's microscopic building blocks could explain the direction of its visible spiral.

Sources indicate that what they discovered was even more remarkable than expected. Rather than forming a single spiral, the tusk's tiny structural components create two intertwined helices that twist in opposite directions. Together, they produce an exceptionally stable structure.

The research was conducted at three major European synchrotron facilities: the Swiss Light Source SLS at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen, the MAX IV Laboratory in Lund (Sweden), and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility ESRF in Grenoble (France). The findings were published in Nature Communications.

A Giant Tooth Built Like Reinforced Concrete.

In a recent development, narwhal tusks continue growing throughout the animals' lives and can easily reach 70 years of age. Despite their striking appearance, the precise purpose of these enormous teeth remains uncertain. Evidence suggests they are primarily involved in mate selection. Narwhals have also been observed crossing their tusks in playful "duels," supporting the idea that the structures are important for reproduction and social interactions.

Although questions remain about how narwhals use their tusks, scientists now have a much clearer picture of how they are constructed.

"Like bones or other teeth in the animal kingdom, the narwhal tusk is a complex composite material whose structure extends from tiny nanoscale building blocks to the visible form of the entire tooth," indicates Marianne Liebi, a PSI researcher and co-author of the study.

Composite materials combine different substances to achieve properties that the individual components cannot provide alone. Reinforced concrete is a familiar example. Concrete made from cement and sand can withstand considerable pressure, while an internal steel framework helps resist pulling forces and provides additional stability.

Industry observers note that "The narwhal tusk, too, must be both hard and flexible," Liebi explains. "Only then can it withstand the strong hydrodynamic forces that swimming generates.".

The Remarkable Microscopic Structure of Narwhal Tusks.

According to recent reports, most of the narwhal's tusk consists of dentin, the same hard tissue that makes up much of the interior of human teeth. A thinner layer of cementum covers its exterior. In other mammals, cementum is typically confined to the roots of teeth.

Industry observers note that both materials contain extremely fine collagen fibers strengthened by tiny mineral crystals. Much like the steel framework inside reinforced concrete, the collagen fibers provide internal reinforcement, while the mineral crystals supply hardness. This combination allows the tusk to possess both strength and flexibility.

Understanding how this microscopic arrangement produces the much larger spiral presented a significant scientific challenge.

"The collagen fibers and mineral crystals are on the nanometer scale, while the spiral of the tooth only becomes visible at centimeter and meter lengths," Marianne Liebi explains.

Sources indicate that A nanometer is one billionth of a meter. To investigate how structures at this incredibly small scale relate to the shape of an entire tusk, the researchers turned to a sophisticated X-ray imaging method known as tensor tomography.

Advanced X-Rays Reveal the Tusk's Hidden Architecture.

Conventional dental X-rays produce images because teeth absorb more radiation than the softer tissues around them. The resulting image is essentially a shadow that reveals the shape and density of the tooth.

However, the powerful X-rays generated at synchrotron research facilities can provide far more detailed information. When these beams encounter regularly organized structures inside a material, the X-rays scatter in distinctive patterns. Scientists can analyze those patterns to determine how microscopic components are arranged.

"From these patterns, we can calculate how the nanometer-sized mineralized collagen fibers inside the material are oriented," explains first author Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo.

It has been revealed that rodriguez-Palomo began working on the project while pursuing his PhD at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden. He subsequently continued the research as a postdoctoral researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark.

Sources indicate that during tensor tomography, researchers rotate the tooth within the synchrotron's X-ray beam while collecting measurements at individual locations. Millions of these measurements are then combined to reconstruct a three-dimensional representation of the tusk's internal organization, connecting its microscopic components with the much larger structure.

An Unexpected Discovery Hidden in the Data.

When the researchers first examined their extensive imaging data, they could not find the spiral structure they had anticipated.

"That puzzled us quite a bit," recalls Marianne Liebi.

Earlier mechanical experiments had indicated that the tusk's characteristic twist should be reflected in the orientation of its collagen fibers and mineral crystals.

"But instead of a helix, all we saw was a regular pattern.".

According to recent reports, the breakthrough came when the scientists changed their approach. Rather than examining individual points in the three-dimensional images in isolation, they investigated how the orientation of each point related to its neighbors.

"When we compared how these points were oriented relative to each other, a directional trend began to appear," recalls Palomo. "All we had to do then was connect the dots - as in a children's paint-by-numbers kit - and suddenly the structure became visible: two intertwined spirals.".

Two Opposing Spirals Give Narwhal Tusks Their Strength.

Industry observers note that further examination revealed that the two spirals occupy different regions of the tooth. The thin outer cementum layer forms a left-handed helix, whereas the mineralized collagen structures within the underlying dentin spiral in the opposite direction.

Sources indicate that this sophisticated natural design provides substantial mechanical advantages. Much like the intertwined strands of a rope, the two opposing helices work together to create an exceptionally stable structure. Their arrangement helps the tusk resist twisting forces, known as torsion, as well as other forms of mechanical stress.

The same microscopic architecture also produces the narwhal's recognizable corkscrew shape, linking the extraordinary appearance of the legendary unicorn horn to structures far too small to see with the naked eye.

Narwhal Tusks Preserve Decades of Arctic History.

The study forms part of a research project funded by NordForsk called "Narwhal tusks - a tale with a twist." It also received support from the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie program.

Under the leadership of Henrik Birkedal of Aarhus University in Denmark, the international and interdisciplinary research team is exploring both the internal architecture of narwhal tusks and the relationship between tusk growth, environmental conditions, and climate.

As a narwhal's tusk grows, it develops successive layers that function much like the annual growth rings of a tree. Scientists can examine these structures to reconstruct past Arctic environmental conditions, including changes in climate and food availability.

During a lifespan that can approach a century, a male narwhal effectively builds its own environmental archive within its remarkable spiral tooth.

Industry observers note that materials provided by Paul Scherrer Institute. Original written by Benjamin A. Senn. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#163302. AI goes from math dunce to genius

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1088 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

AI goes from math dunce to genius

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that last year, I asked ChatGPT to add up my British state pension contributions.
  • It has been revealed that A friend who teaches math wasn't surprised.
  • Fast-forward to November 2026, and a mathematician working at artificial intelligence firm Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, claims to have solved one of the hardest problems in mathematical history with the help of the company's chatbot, Claude.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last year, I asked ChatGPT to add up my British state pension contributions. Thankfully, I double-checked. The total was wrong by a few pounds.

It has been revealed that A friend who teaches math wasn't surprised. Chatbots, he noted, often get simple calculations wrong.

Fast-forward to November 2026, and a mathematician working at artificial intelligence firm Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, claims to have solved one of the hardest problems in mathematical history with the help of the company's chatbot, Claude.

That problem was the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers, and has baffled mathematicians since 1859.

How did AI go from stumbling over simple arithmetic to scaling such extraordinary mathematical heights?

The answer lies in how AI processes information, remarked Andrea Asperti, a professor in computer science at Italy's University of Bologna.

Unlike conventional calculators, early chatbots were trained to predict language, producing plausible answers without necessarily doing the math.

Ironically, they may perform millions of calculations to arrive at the wrong answer.

"In a sense, asking why a chatbot makes arithmetic mistakes despite its enormous computational power is like asking why humans make mistakes in mental arithmetic despite having billions of neurons in their brains," Asperti told DW.

Ken Ono, a mathematics professor at the University of Virginia in the United States, recalled how Google's Gemini once concluded that 9.11 was greater than 9.8.

"But make no mistake, those errors are very rare today," Ono told DW.

Asperti attributed AI's gains to gradual improvements in model size, training data and methods rather than a single breakthrough.

AI can now explore different approaches, check its work, correct mistakes and use specialized computational tools.

"What is remarkable is that these relatively incremental technological improvements have resulted in qualitative leaps in intellectual capabilities," Asperti said.

Perhaps most surprising was AI's ability to solve previously unsolved problems — something many had doubted it could do.

"Solving open mathematical problems requires a considerable degree of creativity: it is not simply a matter of retrieving existing knowledge or reproducing known arguments," Asperti mentioned.

Kevin Buzzard, a mathematician at Imperial College London, UK, was excited but not surprised by the proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis.

He had already seen AI resolve a problem in algebraic geometry by finding a counterexample.

According to recent reports, "I had thought about the problem myself and could see what the difficulties were. AI cut through them," Buzzard told DW.

Ono draws an analogy with chess: While humans struggle to think several moves ahead, AI can explore countless possibilities. In advanced mathematics, the scope is far greater.

According to recent reports, "When it comes to pure mathematics, there are tens of thousands of research papers that are the individual moves that it gets to play with. And what we're seeing is the power of that capacity," Ono stated.

Another advantage is AI's ability to recognize connections across different areas of mathematics.

"Most of us become specialists, building upon theories that we learn over time. And it's difficult to become proficient in many more than a small handful of areas," Ono said.

The proposed Riemann proof illustrates that breadth. "It might be 30 or 40 mathematicians you would have to put in a room before you could assemble this proof," he said.

And AI's knowledge extends well beyond math.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Ono suggested that the mathematician behind the Claude-assisted proof could have interrupted his work to ask the chatbot: "Hey, by the way, next week I'm going to Hawaii. Come up with a beautiful itinerary for a long weekend in Hawaii.".

He and Claude could then have seamlessly returned to advanced mathematics.

"The point I make there is that Claude seems to know everything at a fairly deep level, and humans don't," Ono noted.

Ono suggests the individual ideas behind the proposed proof may all be within human intellectual reach.

"But the sheer scope and the ability to assemble ideas that had never been assembled before, that is what is extraordinary here," he mentioned.

Ono called the achievement "superhuman.".

Asperti believes AI could develop an entirely different kind of mathematical intuition.

Mathematicians work with abstract spaces of hundreds or thousands of dimensions, which humans, living in a three-dimensional world, struggle to visualize.

AI might develop its own ways of understanding such structures and "discover relationships that are difficult for us even to imagine," Asperti stated.

Ono is excited about the future of mathematics but concerned about the future of mathematicians.

Until recently, he would have discouraged young mathematicians from tackling problems like the Riemann hypothesis, saying they could spend 20 years without producing any results.

"Shoot for the moon! The bar has been raised so high that if your primary interest as a mathematician is in the questions themselves, then this is a great time.".

"The flip side, if you're a mathematician and your identity is that you want to be the source of the ideas, well, you may have lost most of that.".

Ono, who has trained 35 PhD students, is "deeply worried" about their future.

"Make no mistake. In the year 2026, the ground shifted beneath the entire edifice of the world of human mathematical research," he mentioned.

Ono believes the role of future mathematicians will be "much more like being a conductor of the most extraordinary orchestra.".

In the past, mathematicians were trained by getting them to prove theorems.

"Now you can prove a theorem by pressing a button," mentioned Buzzard, "so we need new methods.".

Buzzard is setting up a lab that emphasizes understanding, explaining and defending complex mathematical arguments.

"The best team for doing mathematics is a computer plus human team, and it is still relatively straightforward to extract insights and understanding from what machines are doing," he said.

But, he remarked, mathematical research may "end up completely dominated by machines doing things which humans simply cannot comprehend any more, very cheaply and at the touch of a button.".

So, that is the concern of solving mathematical problems. What about AI's ability to come up with mathematical problems and propositions, like an Albert Einstein?

Ono noted: "If you trained a large language model on all the mathematics and all the physics that was known by the end of the 19th century, would a model spin up Einstein's theory of relativity on its own? I don't think we've seen that sort of creative spark, that sort of ability yet.".

Some U.S. food banks see demand top pandemic levels

💡 Key Takeaways
  • During the Covid-19 pandemic, Greg Silverman watched an MTA bus driver pull over on Manhattan's Upper West Side, let his passengers off and run across the street toward him.
  • Silverman, who runs Newly introduced York nonprofit West Side Campaign Against Hunger, initially thought the driver wanted to use the bathroom at the church where the food distribution was taking place.
  • Industry observers note that "He was a full-time employee," Silverman mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the Covid-19 pandemic, Greg Silverman watched an MTA bus driver pull over on Manhattan's Upper West Side, let his passengers off and run across the street toward him.

Silverman, who runs Newly introduced York nonprofit West Side Campaign Against Hunger, initially thought the driver wanted to use the bathroom at the church where the food distribution was taking place. Instead, the man asked, "Can I get some food?".

Industry observers note that "He was a full-time employee," Silverman mentioned. "You are an essential personnel, making the city survive and you need food.".

Now, Silverman stated, his organization has seen demand surpass even the levels it observed during that time of crisis when the U.S. economy ground to a halt — and many of the people now seeking food also have jobs. Silverman expects the nonprofit to distribute as much as 6 million pounds of food this year.

"The height of the pandemic was not the height of need, by any means," he said.

In a recent development, the pressure on the emergency food system extends beyond Latest York. Nationally, use of charitable food programs remains elevated as sustained inflation makes it harder for Americans to afford food, housing and healthcare. Higher prices come at the same time that the federal government has restricted food aid.

Recent findings suggest that the Department of Agriculture's latest annual report found that 13.7% of U.S. households, roughly 18.3 million households, experienced food insecurity in 2024. That rate was significantly higher than in every year from 2016 through 2021.

Recent findings suggest that the pandemic initially brought a surge in demand for charitable food programs, which was followed by government support. In the years that followed, pandemic-era policies such as expanded Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits, the enhanced child tax credit and school meal programs phased out as inflation spiked.

Industry observers note that "This is not because you can't go to work," remarked City Harvest President Carlos Rodriguez. "Primarily, your work and your wages are just not keeping up with the way costs have gone up in the last five years alone.".

Sources indicate that city Harvest, which works with food providers across the five boroughs of Fresh York, told CNBC 1 in 5 New Yorkers is currently experiencing food insecurity, or limited access to enough food because of a lack of money or other resources. That is up from 1 in 6 a year earlier, and 1 in 8 before the pandemic.

Average monthly visits to food pantries and soup kitchens in New York are also 85% higher than before the pandemic, mentioned Rodriguez.

In the Federal Reserve's October Beige Book, the central bank's Fresh York regional branch described a sharp rise in first-time food pantry people. One nonprofit leader told the Federal Reserve Bank of New York that the strain was comparable to the pandemic, "but without the same philanthropic and government support.".

Data from Plentiful, a technology platform that connects people with food pantries and tracks their usage, also points to growing demand and limited resources.

According to recent reports, "For pantries using our reservation and pre-registration features, we see that the overwhelming majority of those are at or over capacity," said Catherine Compitello, CEO of Plentiful. "Demand is growing while supply is not.".

Recent findings suggest that first-time users of Plentiful in Latest York City rose roughly 56% from August to October, Compitello said. It was the second-largest fall surge since 2016; the only larger one came during last year's federal government shutdown, when delayed SNAP benefits drove more people to seek food assistance.

Compitello said that when families have trouble affording essentials, they often prioritize healthcare, transportation, childcare and utilities, leaving food as the expense they cut back on.

Demand for food banks is rising in other regions of the country, and nonprofits are facing their own operational challenges as they try to meet it.

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank told CNBC the organization's diesel bill more than doubled in September, to roughly $75,000, adding to the cost of delivering food and running refrigerated trucks.

It has been revealed that demand in the region is also spiking. Distribution in the Los Angeles area for January through September totaled 116 million pounds of food and grocery products — the equivalent of 93 million meals — and slightly higher than a near-record year in 2025, according to the Los Angeles Regional Food Bank.

Industry observers note that federal food aid changes have exacerbated the problems. Rodriguez of City Harvest described SNAP as a first line of defense against hunger, saying the program can provide as many as nine meals for every one meal the organization provides. But City Harvest has estimated at least 8.7% of SNAP recipients in Fresh York City lost benefits over the past year, after congressional Republicans and President Donald Trump approved work certification requirements and changes to eligibility.

The pressure is also mounting in Los Angeles County, where roughly 260,000 CalFresh recipients are subject to expanded federal work requirements that took effect in June. CalFresh is California's version of SNAP.

In a recent development, that does not mean all 260,000 will lose benefits, since people who meet the work requirements or qualify for an exemption can remain eligible. But a Los Angeles Regional Food Bank spokesperson told CNBC the changes add another layer of uncertainty for households already struggling with food costs.

According to recent reports, in Atlanta, the pressure extends beyond the city itself to the surrounding region. The Atlanta Community Food Bank serves about 270,000 households a month, or nearly 700,000 people, through partner pantries across North Georgia. President and CEO Kyle Waide said the number of people it serves has jumped more than 70% in five years.

"Much of that increase is among people whose incomes are too high to qualify for federal benefit programs," noted Waide.

Under current SNAP guidelines in Georgia, most households must have gross monthly income at or below 130% of the federal poverty level to qualify. They must also meet a separate net income test. For fiscal 2027, which began Oct. 1, the gross income limit is $2,960 a month for a household of three, or about $35,520 annually, and $3,575 a month for a household of four, or $42,900 a year.

According to recent reports, more than 60% of Atlanta Community Food Bank clients have household incomes above the cutoff for SNAP eligibility, Waide said, generally in the mid-to-upper $30,000 range depending on household size. The food bank does not collect everyone's income, he said, but the figure is based on survey estimates.

Given those dynamics, Waide said he does not expect the need to ease.

Industry observers note that "We're preparing for the level of demand to stay where it is today, or even increase more," Waide said. "We don't see a big source of relief coming anytime soon.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.

It has been revealed that although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China. In a press release, however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security.

The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Among crimes, Huawei was found guilty of “repeatedly” lying to banks about its business in Iran. Huawei also frequently lied to the US government that “it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ said. In reality, the DOJ proved at trial that Huawei was conducting business in Iran under the name “Skycom” to evade sanctions, while providing Iran with “turnkey services with respect to an Internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks.” Further, Huawei helped the Iranian regime “monitor and censor its people’ access to the Internet” and provided surveillance cameras to monitor protests, the DOJ said. In a statement, the acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, M. Scott Proctor, said Huawei “empowered our enemies” and “harmed our national security.”.

Sources indicate that as the DOJ successfully argued, Huawei lied about its Iranian business specifically so that it could continue obtaining billions in US dollars by participating in a global marketplace that gave it necessary access to steal US tech. Among companies targeted, US Attorney for the Eastern District of New York Joseph Nocella Jr. said that Huawei blatantly stole from T-Mobile and Cisco, as well as a semiconductor storage company called CNEX and an antenna manufacturer called Quintel.

One of the stolen ideas was the design of a T-Mobile robot called “Tappy,” which helped the US firm “assess the responsiveness of touch screens by mimicking a human touch,” the DOJ said. To copy the design, Huawei signed a non-disclosure agreement, then sent photos and technical details back to China. Even bolder, when that intel was deemed insufficient, “a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DOJ said.

Huawei’s tactics weren’t always sophisticated, but they were effective, the DOJ said, building into “a long-running conspiracy to steal intellectual property of US companies.” At trade highlights and tours of rivals’ facilities, Huawei employees would pretend to “get lost,” the DOJ said, so they could wander into restricted areas and take photos of hardware, The Latest York Times reported.

According to recent reports, huawei engineers would also sometimes hide their activity by spelling words backwards. For example, Huawei was able to copy the source code used on Cisco routers—which the DOJ mentioned was “identified as the ‘crown jewel’ of Cisco technology”—by taking notes in which they spelled Cisco as “ocsic.” Another time, the DOJ noted that a Huawei employee was caught “photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment” while wearing a badge that falsely identified him as an employee of “Weihua.”.

During the trial, Meredith Arfa, a federal prosecutor, noted that Huawei employees were sometimes paid bonuses for their crimes, since the theft was so integral to Huawei’s business model, NYT reported.

Roman Rozhavsky, the assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, mentioned that Huawei spent years expanding its international enterprise “through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of US companies and the rule of law.”.

Huawei has been banned from selling its tech in the US since 2019, so NYT noted that the guilty verdict is unlikely to rattle the company’s finances much. However, the financial penalties stemming from the verdict could be steep, as the DOJ explained that they include “criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution.”.

Sentencing is scheduled for September 14.

Huawei continues to deny any wrongdoing and rejects US claims that the Chinese Communist Party directed the thefts. NYT noted that Huawei’s investors have argued that the US fight is politically motivated and seeks to hobble “a Chinese initiative to build 5G networks around the world.”.

In a recent development, outside the courthouse following the verdict, Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that it’s significant that the jury did not convict Huawei of racketeering charges or conspiracy to obstruct justice. According to Heberlig, the examples of US technology theft merely represented “isolated misconduct by organization employees,” which inevitably happens in a company so large, with “hundreds of thousands of people.”.

Heberlig confirmed that Huawei planned to appeal and considered the jury’s opposition to racketeering charges to be a “profound rejection of the United States’ narratives about what Huawei is.”.

“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hard-working company that we came to know and deeply respect in this trial,” Heberlig stated.

Recent findings suggest that after the verdict, China “lashed out” at the US, AFP reported. According to Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, the US is trying to use the ruling to “suppress” Huawei.

China “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises and firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests,” Guo remarked.

However, the FBI’s Rozhavsky suggested that even China, which frequently negotiates with Trump as the trade rivals continually clash, can’t spare Huawei from substantial penalties.

“This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation,” Rozhavsky said. “No tech giant is too substantial, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the US and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”.

#163297. How East Germany boosted Vietnam's coffee industry

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1046 w)

How East Germany boosted Vietnam's coffee industry

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coffee lovers, brace yourselves: Imagine taking your first sip, expecting the rich aroma of roasted coffee beans, only to discover that your cup contains a concoction made from ingredients you can barely identify.
  • That's exactly what millions of outraged East Germans experienced in 1977.
  • A poor harvest in Brazil saw global coffee prices skyrocketing, creating a major problem for East Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee lovers, brace yourselves: Imagine taking your first sip, expecting the rich aroma of roasted coffee beans, only to discover that your cup contains a concoction made from ingredients you can barely identify.

That's exactly what millions of outraged East Germans experienced in 1977. But what led to this?

A poor harvest in Brazil saw global coffee prices skyrocketing, creating a major problem for East Germany. Unlike West Germany's Deutsche Mark, the East German Mark was a domestic currency with no value abroad.

Sources indicate that even under normal circumstances, the country constantly struggled to obtain the hard currency it needed to pay for imports. In 1974 and 1975, East Germany spent around 150 million Valutamarks — the term used in East Germany for the West German Deutsche Mark — on imported coffee. The following year, it had to pay almost five times as much.

It has been revealed that however, this rate of inflation could not be passed on to consumers because, "In the GDR, there was the dogma of stable prices — set by the state through law," explains historian Stefan Wolle, a consultant at the DDR Museum in Berlin (DDR is the acronym used for East Germany in German). "Prices were set by the Politburo, not by businesses. And they weren't allowed to change. What sounds wonderfully socially minded at first glance had serious negative economic consequences, because production costs were far higher than retail prices.".

The government needed a solution. On August 1, 1977, it introduced "Kaffee Mix" as a substitute for popular coffee brands back then such as Kosta, Rondo and Mocca Fix. The fine print on the packaging promised "a blend of select green coffee beans and carefully balanced coffee substitutes.".

Recent findings suggest that in plain English, that meant 51% of the blend consisted of imported coffee beans. The rest was a mixture of rye and barley, along with chicory and either spelt or sugar beet. It tasted disgusting, Wolle recalls.

Recent findings suggest that even the coffee machines appeared to reject the concoction. The mixture expanded and clogged the filters in cafeterias and restaurants. Some machines were even mentioned to have exploded.

Public discontent boiled over during this "coffee crisis." People responded by boycotting the product, and with biting sarcasm, too: "The difference between a neutron bomb and coffee mix: There isn't one — the cup stays intact, but the person is destroyed.".

Sources indicate that A sharper dig? "It's pure rat poison.".

According to recent reports, more than 14,000 complaint letters poured into government offices. On September 1, the Ministry for State Security, better known as the Stasi, reported to the leadership of the ruling Socialist Unity Party of Germany or SED, that Kaffee Mix was being "rejected by broad sections of the population." (Editor's note: The SED was the only ruling party in East Germany then).

To understand the intensity of the backlash, it's vital to recognize coffee's special place in East German society.

"Coffee was, in a way, the social glue that held together East Germany's particular brand of conviviality and camaraderie," claims Wolle.

During the 1960s and 1970s, people would gather for coffee after lunch, often accompanied by homemade cakes or treats from the bakery. "It was a sacred hour in every workplace and office. It was a huge mistake for the SED leadership to slaughter this sacred cow, so to speak.".

Recent findings suggest that according to Wolle, real coffee was still occasionally available in the larger cities. But in smaller towns and rural areas, people often had no choice but to make do with Kaffee Mix. East Germans who had relatives or friends in West Germany and regularly received packages from them could count themselves lucky.

"Our relatives and friends in the West knew what was in short supply in East Germany, so they would usually include a substantial bag of good West German coffee," Wolle recalls.

It is estimated that around 25% of all coffee consumed in East Germany came from the West. During the height of the coffee crisis, that share was briefly even higher.

"Of course, the SED leadership had mixed feelings about people receiving so many packages from the West," Wolle states. "Police officers and full-time party officials weren't allowed to have contacts in the West. But ordinary citizens didn't care.".

Especially after the blend stirred up such negative reactions.

It has been revealed that east Germany's leaders responded by looking to their socialist allies in Africa for help. They negotiated special agreements with Angola and Ethiopia.

Sources indicate that "Instead of paying in hard currency, they paid with military equipment — weapons and trucks," Wolle explains. "Weapons that were used in Ethiopia's civil war.".

But the East German leadership sought a long-term solution, and eventually established a partnership with another socialist ally: Vietnam.

It has been revealed that "Coffee had already been grown there under French colonial rule," states Wolle. "People knew that coffee grew well there and that the quality was good.".

Recent findings suggest that starting in the 1980s, East Germany invested heavily in developing the infrastructure needed for large-scale coffee cultivation in Vietnam, Wolle explains. It supplied machinery and equipment, built transportation routes, and provided housing for plantation workers. "There was just one catch: Coffee plants take several years before they can be harvested.".

By the time the plants were finally ready to produce coffee, the Berlin Wall had fallen and East Germany was a thing of the past.

"But the Vietnamese benefited enormously," states Wolle. "They converted the plantations into private enterprises fairly quickly." Today, Vietnam is one of the world's largest coffee exporters. "What's surprising is that most people don't even know that.".

There’s no mention of it on the packages — and if there is, it’s in microscopic print.

"The Vietnamese don’t make a big deal out of their role because they themselves probably still believe that coffee has to come from Brazil — or at least from Latin America — to be any good," states Wolle.

Passionate coffee drinkers may not care where the hot beverage comes from — as long as it doesn't taste like spelt and sugar beets, as the much-maligned East German Kaffee Mix once did.

This article was originally written in German.

Best Traditional Espresso Machine in our guide to the best, the Mio is stylish and built to last, with an analog design and a two-year warranty. It also makes for a solid first “real” espresso machine with its built-in shot timer and pressure gauge.

According to recent reports, fellow set some pretty lofty expectations with the release of its sleek Aiden coffee maker in 2024, and according to former WIRED reviewer and espresso expert Matthew Korfhage, the brand didn't disappoint on its first attempt at an espresso machine. The ability to adjust flow rates and pressure curves was once the province of, as Korfhage put it, only the “richest and nerdiest of nerds.” But Fellow now allows you—yes, you, at home in your kitchen—to fine-tune how water moves through the grounds, unlocking previously unforeseen dimensions of flavor.

When we tested this machine, we liked it for a variety of reasons, including an easy-to-use milk frother and two swappable bean hoppers, which are especially helpful if you like to switch to decaf in the afternoons. It comes in a variety of finishes, but note that Beige is the cheapest of all right now, at only $915.

Recent findings suggest that this flashy, design-oriented semiautomatic (“a steampunk gasworks of a thing,” according to Korfhage) is quite dramatic in person. It has a dual boiler—meaning you can froth milk at the same time you’re pulling a shot—and it comes with a nice set of accessories, including a tamper and milk pitcher. Note that this sale is on the second-gen machine, which features expanded grinder settings and a new portafilter.

The Best Semiautomatic Machine for Most People, the Barista Express is a longtime Reviews team favorite and platonic ideal of an espresso machine, with its pressure gauge and industrial-looking steam wand. If you want a built-in grinder without dropping four figures, this is your machine and your sale.

In a recent development, formerly the Linea Classic, De’Longhi’s Classic is the best bare-bones espresso machine we’ve tried, with a pressure gauge, 15-bar pump, and updated thermoblock system. I used one for a full year and, while it’s not as foolproof as a semiautomatic, it was easy enough for morning espresso shots and cappuccinos; I even pulled off some rudimentary latte art with its steam wand.

Sources indicate that the Vertuo Pop+ is our favorite pod maker for espresso. The Deluxe model adds a larger, side-mount water tank (37 ounces to the original’s 25 ounces) and new finishes, including this white one, a matte black-and-gold, and a sort of gunmetal gray.

Latest Update: Russia sports ban: Ukraine's Heraskevych hails EU pushback

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych has welcomed a move by the European Union to take a tougher stance on Russian athletes competing in the 27-member bloc.
  • According to recent reports, heraskevych is one of the most outspoken critics of Russia's reintegration into international sport.
  • On Monday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed banning Russian athletes from competing under their own flag at sports competitions within the European Union and urged member states to consider denying visas in such cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych has welcomed a move by the European Union to take a tougher stance on Russian athletes competing in the 27-member bloc.

According to recent reports, heraskevych is one of the most outspoken critics of Russia's reintegration into international sport. He made headlines at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina when he was disqualified for his helmet honoring Ukrainian athletes killed in the war with Russia.

On Monday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed banning Russian athletes from competing under their own flag at sports competitions within the European Union and urged member states to consider denying visas in such cases.

"Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities," she said.

In an interview with DW, Heraskevych described the EU move as coming "better late than never.".

"We waited a long time for this backlash," he said at the International Bobsleigh and Skeleton Federation World Cup in Altenberg, Germany, his first competition since the Winter Olympics.

"I'm really happy to see that people start to care about sports and they understand the value of sports as a huge platform," he added.

It has been revealed that in July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) paved the way for Russia's full return to international sport by ending its recommendation that Russian athletes be allowed to compete as neutrals, without their flag, colors or anthems. The IOC also noted Russian teams should be allowed to return to international competition.

Several major Olympic sports, such as swimming and gymnastics, have already fully reinstated Russia, despite the country's ongoing attacks on Ukraine.

"It makes no sense to me," Heraskevych noted.

However, in recent weeks there has been a growing European pushback against the easing of Russia's sporting isolation.

Industry observers note that among the catalysts was a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to overturn a ban on Russia in international ice hockey. That prompted seven European countries to say they would refuse to play against Russia, while Germany, at one point, remarked withdrawing as host of next year's men's world championship was an option.

The dispute over the CAS ruling drew a response from the Kremlin.

"It is a flagrant violation of the Olympic Charter [the IOC's rulebook] and leads toward the destruction of Olympism as a whole," Russian President Vladimir Putin said in China last week.

"Sport, like art, should bring people together.".

Meanwhile, a group of Nordic and Baltic countries want the EU to go even further, pushing for an immediate EU-wide visa ban on all Russian athletes.

"The matter is too urgent to wait until [newly introduced visa rules] enter into force," the leaders of Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Sweden wrote in a November 23 letter to von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

"From my perspective, the IOC is in a very massive crisis," Heraskevych mentioned, referencing the European pushback.

Blanket bans could have a huge effect on qualifying events in Europe for the 2028 Los Angeles Summer Olympics.

Sources indicate that under its president, Kirsty Coventry, the IOC has sought to bring Russia, an Olympic powerhouse, back in from the cold. Coventry has argued that athletes shouldn't be punished for the actions of their governments, and the IOC has strengthened its political neutrality rules in the Olympic Charter.

However, Heraskevych takes exception to the idea that sport should be kept out of politics.

"We are not living in a bubble," he noted.

"Already more than 800 people who were part of the sport family in Ukraine were killed. Ukrainian hockey stadiums, Ukrainian swimming pools, anything related to sports have also been attacked. So we cannot separate sport and politics in Ukraine. The same way Russian sport is involved in politics.".

Recent findings suggest that critics have accused Coventry of cozying up to Russia. In September, it emerged that she had written a letter to Mikhail Degtyarev, Russia's sports minister and president of the Russian Olympic Committee, wishing him luck ahead of an international sports forum.

In a recent development, degtyarev has been sanctioned by the EU. The IOC has declined to comment on the letter but not denied its existence.

Heraskevych said he was not "angry" with any particular Russian athlete, and even floated the idea of a team of Russian refugees.

"I am not against peaceful athletes competing," he said.

"They should be part of competition only if they are part of a refugee team. So, if they have refugee status in another country, and if they condemn the war that Russia started in Ukraine.".

Industry News: Finland's Prime Minister Sanna Marin concedes election

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 2 min read (490 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.
  • The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data revealed with all ballots counted.
  • “We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo stated in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data revealed with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo stated in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job.

It has been revealed that “We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister mentioned in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive new leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash.

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

The NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has said he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

The Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

The tiny BSW is a party in crisis, as it is set to hand the far-right AfD power in eastern Germany

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this fledgling party has experienced many highs and lows in quick succession.
  • According to recent reports, since October 2026, the acronym BSW has instead stood for theAlliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason.
  • Even more painful for the BSW was its defeat in the German general election in February 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this fledgling party has experienced many highs and lows in quick succession. Released in January 2024, it was named the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) to capitalize on the high profile and momentum of its founder, a former communist who had just exited the socialist Left party.

According to recent reports, since October 2026, the acronym BSW has instead stood for theAlliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason. In the past 34 months the newcomer party celebrated election successes at the European Parliament level and in German state elections. In the eastern states of Brandenburg and Thuringia, the party even took part in governing coalitions; however, both of these collapsed relatively swiftly.

Even more painful for the BSW was its defeat in the German general election in February 2025. The party failed to gain the 5% share of votes required to enter parliament, by less than 10,000 votes. With that, it was denied the country's most key political stage and took the matter to court, demanding a complete recount.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But Germany's Constitutional Court dismissed the BSW's election challenge as inadmissible, pointing to a lack of evidence.

"Simply insinuating the possibility of voting errors or expressing an unproven assumption does not meet the requirements for claiming an electoral mistake," the court explained.

The court's decision was published about a week before the party's federal conference is due to be held in Dresden, the capital of the eastern state of Saxony.

"Germany's election scrutiny process resembles that of a 'banana republic'," was the angry reaction of former party leader Sahra Wagenknecht, who stepped back from frontline leadership of her eponymous party in December 2025. Since then, she has led its commission on fundamental values.

One of her successors at the top of the BSW is European Parliament lawmaker Fabio De Masi. In his view, the decision of the Constitutional Court was a "black day for democracy in Germany.".

Fellow co-leader Amira Mohamed Ali did not want to accept the rejected recount.

"It remains unclear whether the Bundestag is correctly composed and whether the approximately 2.5 million BSW voters have unjustly been deprived of their parliamentary representation," she remarked.

It has been revealed that the disappointment at the failure to enter the Bundestag runs deep. The party has not recovered from this setback. It again failed to win representation in 4 out of 5 state parliaments in elections this year, albeit narrowly.

In Baden-Württemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate, as well as in the city-state of Hamburg in 2025, the BSW received less than 2%. This clearly indicates that it is politically irrelevant in the western German states.

They find themselves in the spotlight, however,  because of the role they are set to play in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the BSW got 5.3% of the vote in September.

Despite being the smallest party in that state parliament, they are set to play a pivotal role. They are the only political party that has indicated a readiness to help the election winner, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), into power.

The AfD, which is classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, won the election with almost 44% of the vote. Although his party does not hold an absolute majority in parliament, lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund wants to be voted Germany's first-ever AfD state premier in December.

Industry observers note that the BSW has not indicated any intention to vote for Siegmund, but if he falls short of winning the absolute majority of 42 votes in the first two rounds of voting, a third round will be held in which a simple majority will suffice to win. The BSW has confirmed aims to abstain from that vote. Siegmund would then only need to pick up one more "yes" vote or abstention.

According to recent reports, during the secret ballot for the state parliament speaker, AfD candidate Tobias Rausch received 9 votes more than his party has lawmakers. It is not known exactly who they came from. Alongside the AfD and BSW, there are 4 other parties in the state parliament: the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), environmentalist Greens, socialist Left Party and center-left Social Democrats (SPD).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will be at the center of the party's upcoming conference in Dresden, because the BSW's increasing closeness with the far-right party is highly controversial.

Several BSW members, including board member Christian Leye, criticized this path in a column published in the weekly Die Zeit.

Leye recalled their party's founding consensus: "The clear political demarcation from the AfD.".

He quoted party founder Wagenknecht, who at that time had remarked: "Of course we will not collude with the AfD.".

"We are starting a party so that all the people who are considering or have voted for the AfD out of anger or disappointment — but not because they are right-wing — have a credible political home," Wagenknecht had continued.

But Wagenknecht has also long argued that the so-called "firewall" policy of mainstream parties refusing to work with the AfD has failed. This is why she is rejecting the idea of entering a mathematically possible governing coalition with the other parties in Saxony-Anhalt.

"We are basically agreed that we neither want to go into coalition with the AfD, nor tolerate them, just as much as we do not want to participate in a firewall coalition," she told German news agency dpa.

How the BSW plans to make its way through this dilemma at its party conference is unclear. Fabio De Masi, who replaced Wagenknecht as co-chair in December 2025, seems well aware of this.

He told German media network RND that dealing with the AfD continued to be like "riding on the edge of a razor blade.".

This article was originally written in German.

Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers.
  • In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.
  • Sources indicate that we see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion.

In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:.

Sources indicate that we see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there’s an incentive to target it.

Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers:.

The second reason that we’ve seen targeting particularly in Russia’s largest data centers or some of Russia’s largest public cloud data centers like Yandex, as well as American hyperscalers that are based in the Gulf, is to impose economic cost in a way that would be disadvantageous for an adversary and would otherwise be quite difficult to impose in other ways. So it’s relatively low cost of munition to high cost of disruption. If you think about the amount of investment that’s been put forward by AWS and other companies in the Gulf to build out these data center installations relative to the cost of the amount of Shahed drones that are manufactured, produced, and utilized by Iran to target these data centers, I would put it very, very conservatively at 100X or even more. The cost ratio is really very lucrative for the adversary, and it provides the opportunity to really degrade the economic outcomes of who you are targeting.

Sources indicate that much of the discussion also focused on cloud resilience lessons for both governments and hyperscalers, with the latter including large cloud and data center operators such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Jarnecki highlighted the example of how Ukraine took steps to safeguard its cloud infrastructure when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military forces to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022:.

I think that Ukraine anticipated this problem set very effectively. They anticipated and understood that Russia would not be discriminating necessarily in its targeting of civilian digital infrastructure particularly, and therefore conducted a large-scale cloud migration at the onset of the full-scale war in part in reaction to the anticipated targeting but then also actual targeting that took place through kinetic means.

Such lessons are vital because 2026 is unlikely to be the last year in which data centers come under substantial military attack, Jarnecki said:.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, I think that this really does indicate a continuation of this kind of targeting, not just because data centers are, despite efforts to harden some of them, relatively squishy, relatively easy to find, and have the potential, because of their complexity, to induce cascading risks within the facility or more widely if they are hit particularly by kinetic munitions. So at present, I would say it’s a dangerous trend that is likely to crop up again.

Throughout the event, Jarnecki also addressed viewer questions about whether data centers can realistically be hardened or built underground to withstand physical attacks, and even how orbital data centers or low-Earth orbit satellite constellations such as Starlink could provide backup options from space.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (537 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Best Buy reports comparable sales growth of 6.1%, highest in five years

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (537 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Best Buy on Tuesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third fiscal quarter and raised its full-year guidance.
  • The consumer electronics retailer reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, a significant beat over expectations of 2.3%, according to market intelligence platform StreetAccount.
  • "We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Best Buy on Tuesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third fiscal quarter and raised its full-year guidance.

The consumer electronics retailer reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, a significant beat over expectations of 2.3%, according to market intelligence platform StreetAccount. The organization mentioned that growth was its highest in five years. It reported a domestic comparable sales increase of 6.2% and international comparable sales growth of 4.9%.

"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about.".

Best Buy also raised its guidance for the rest of the year. It's now expecting full-year revenue of between $43 billion and $43.3 billion compared with a previous expectation of between $42.3 billion and $42.8 billion. It's expecting comparable sales to be up 3.4% to 4% compared with prior guidance of between 1.9% and 3%.

The earnings report is the company's first since Bonfig took over as CEO from Corie Barry at the beginning of the month.

Bonfig said the retailer saw overperformance in both computing and gaming for the quarter, driven by recent game launches and a targeted product assortment.

Looking ahead into the holiday season, he stated the Best Buy consumer remains "resilient," but that they are focused on getting value wherever they can.

"We did see not only our current customers continue to be engaged, but we actually did see more fresh customers come into the brand, as well as we had some customers that we re-engaged as well," Bonfig said. "So those are really, really positive signs for us in Q3, and all of that was factored into the way that we guided for Q4 and the rest of the year.".

Here's how the manufacturer performed in the period ended Oct. 31 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Best Buy reported net income of $353 million, or $1.66 per share, compared with $140 million, or 66 cents per share, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including restructuring charges, Best Buy posted adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share.

It has been revealed that revenue rose to $10.24 billion from $9.67 billion in the year-ago period. Best Buy reported domestic revenue of $9.42 billion and international revenue of $820 million.

Tuesday's earnings are the latest in a series of strong reports from the retailer, which has been instituting a turnaround strategy to return to growth after getting hit by declining foot traffic, lower consumer sentiment, tariffs and memory costs.

Shares of Best Buy are up nearly 45% this year.

In a recent development, bonfig told CNBC last quarter that the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" in the current quarter is expected to drive sales in the gaming category, which has been seeing gains over the past year. Last month, Best Buy released a fresh gaming experience for customers featuring gaming content, technology and special offers, among other features.

"I think there'll still be opportunities for gaming to continue to drive our business moving forward," Bonfig told CNBC on Tuesday.

Industry News: Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss.
  • Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022.
  • According to recent reports, the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

According to recent reports, the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

Sources indicate that this resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled plans to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” said Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a big re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole mentioned.

The euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

Industry observers note that A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

It has been revealed that jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, noted he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s plans and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

“In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he said.

The Vice President of the Philippines, Sara Duterte, criticized the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Thursday, saying it would not provide a fair trial for her ex-president father's crimes against humanity case.

She remarked the court would try to "make a statement.".

Former President Rodrigo Duterte has been detained at The Hague since his arrest on an ICC warrant in March 2025, over extra-judicial killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.

Recent findings suggest that the trial begins on Monday, where Rodrigo Duterte is expected to plead not guilty. Witnesses will be called up to testify the next day, with more than 500 alleged victims represented in ⁠court.

Recent findings suggest that "I think the ICC, after the ganging up of superpowers, (will) want to make a statement that they are in the right. So there is no-one else there that they would like to make a statement to. And that's the case of Rodrigo Duterte," said his daughter Sara.

Duterte stated "China, Russia and our BFF the United States," all considered the ICC a "political organization" and not an impartial arbiter.

BFF stands for "best friend forever" and was likely a swipe at the Philippines' close ties with the US under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

Prosecutors at the ICC ​accuse the 81-year-old former president of funding and arming execution squads that murdered as many as 30,000 people.

He has been charged with three counts of crimes against ​humanity involving murder and attempted murder between 2011 and 2018.

In a recent development, duterte is the first Asian former ​leader and only ‌the second former national ruler to appear before the court for crimes allegedly committed while in power. The other one was Laurent Gbagbo of Ivory Coast, who was ultimately acquitted in 2019.

Supporters of the former president, who was arrested in Manila, say he was "kidnapped" and sent to The Hague after his daughter had a bitter falling-out with current president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., with whom she had held an alliance that helped him win a landslide 2022 election victory.

The younger Duterte is also facing an ongoing impeachment trial in the Philippine Senate and if found guilty, she would be barred permanently from elected office.

She noted both her case and her father's ICC trial were related to efforts to make her ineligible to run for the 2028 presidential election.

It has been revealed that "I still believe that it's about the 2028 elections, whether there will be elections or there will be no elections. It's about the change of leadership, if there will ever be a change of leadership," she told reporters.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the manufacturer to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.
  • In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the firm’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”.
  • “Our recent terms patch was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the manufacturer to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.

In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the firm’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”.

“Our recent terms patch was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”.

Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the manufacturer had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere “sugar coating.”.

He stated he still plans on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1.

Sources indicate that “I would say I’m losing 20 percent of my yearly income,” he stated. “It’s a few mortgage payments.”.

He noted that Etsy’s announcement also seems to be rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season.

“This is the worst two-to-three weeks out of the year to do this, bar none,” he said.

Industry observers note that the fracas began earlier this month, when the tech giant first proposed fresh contractual language. The updated terms read:.

As a result, a slew of vendors pulled up stakes, with some saying they had “burned their Etsy shop to the ground” or that they “just killed our Etsy store after 13 years.”.

Etsy’s change is reminiscent of a recent dust-up involving Meta, where the tech giant had wanted to “require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.” Meta then indefinitely paused that move.

Last month, Etsy also told sellers that it would “set clearer restrictions on AI use,” despite the fact that AI-generated items remain for sale all over the site.

“Today, many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content,” James Ossman, the firm’s vice president of customer operations, wrote on October 22. “It’s become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.”.

For years, Etsy has been notoriously poor at enforcing its own rules, not only regarding AI but also the official prohibitions on selling sex toys, pornography, and even purported witchcraft spells.
