📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johanna, 24, began questioning her ADHD diagnosis when she discovered it could act as a barrier to becoming a police officer.

Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.

In a recent development, countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.

But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.

This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.

At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.

Industry observers note that but as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.

Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.

"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.

If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

Sources indicate that the existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable â and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.

Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.

Psychologist Sebastian LundstrÃ¶m runs the clinic, which operates one day a month.

Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.

This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.

Industry observers note that since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (Â£1,100) privately.

When Freya was referred to the clinic, she claims she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.

Sources indicate that johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.

But as she grew into adulthood, she claims she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.

Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.

It has been revealed that johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.

Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.

The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.

"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian LundstrÃ¶m, the clinic's lead psychologist.

The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the newly introduced assessment.

LundstrÃ¶m says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.

But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not right now showing symptoms is a contested approach.

"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," notes Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism SkÃ¥ne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.

"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.

Symptoms could reappear later in life, he notes. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support.".

LundstrÃ¶m claims he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.

During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnoses but the psychologist mentioned, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".

Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis as she feels she was misdiagnosed.

Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.

"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it.".

It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, LundstrÃ¶m explains.

According to recent reports, "It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he states. It is only open one day a month.

Recent findings suggest that before opening the clinic, LundstrÃ¶m conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.

"It's key to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to LundstrÃ¶m, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.

The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.

Recent findings suggest that "It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she claims. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way.".

In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.

Freya notes she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

Industry observers note that but the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.

Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism SkÃ¥ne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people, says it is important to remember autism and ADHD are lifelong conditions.

The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," states Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister VÃ¤sternorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.

"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.

Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.

Eric Donell, the chairman of RiksfÃ¶rbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely notable. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he indicates.

Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.

People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, states LundstrÃ¶m, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.

Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".

"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she claims.

Instead, she indicates, her colleagues belittled her.

Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.

The Swedish reassessment clinic claims they generally would not apply upcoming or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.

Sources indicate that "The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.

It has been revealed that back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.

She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.

"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else.".

It has been revealed that we’re on the hunt for researchers and founders who are engineering solutions to some of the most formidable problems society faces, including human disease and climate change. In a recent development, have someone in mind? Or think you’d be a great candidate and want to nominate yourself? Follow this link to suggest someone who you think should make our 2027 list. It’s free and takes only a few minutes. Just be sure to get your nomination in before the deadline—which is 11:59 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, January 19.

After the deadline, our editors will review all nominees and select a group of semifinalists, whom we’ll invite to complete a formal application. Then, dozens of expert judges will help us evaluate those applicants and settle on the finalists. You can read more about our selection process here.

We look forward to reviewing your nominations.

#163170. From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices

From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working.
  • It has been revealed that as Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices.
  • As an apartment dweller in Upcoming York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.

It has been revealed that as Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:.

As an apartment dweller in Upcoming York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.

I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).

Accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.

My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.

Recent findings suggest that I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.

Recent findings suggest that aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).

In a recent development, last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.

Greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”.

My current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.

Industry observers note that the monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.

Below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.

The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.

The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.

I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.

The primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel issues, and this thing has been a lifesaver.

I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.

Industry observers note that above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.

I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.

Industry observers note that to combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.

My desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.

According to recent reports, on the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. At the moment that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.

The right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.

Since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.

Industry observers note that I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.

When I built the shelf for my desk, I fabricated a mounting bracket for the arm out of schedule 40 steel pipe and a 3D-printed sleeve that sits in a pocket CNC’d out. Since it sits flush on the underside, I don’t have to use a clamp that would extend down into the space where I keep my Mac and audio interface.

It has been revealed that when I need a secondary display, or I want to use my Apple Pencil in Photoshop or Illustrator, I use an iPad Pro. I used to have a dedicated Wacom monitor, but I find this much more convenient both in terms of space efficiency and ergonomics. If I’m not really leaning into hand drawing or lettering, I do most of my graphic work with a mouse, which is currently a Logitech MX Master 3S.

According to recent reports, to wrap up the final items, the chair is an Aeron I bought new in 2003. I’ve had to repair it a few times over the years, but it’s either been things I consider wear items (wheels, armrests, gas cylinder) or Herman Miller has replaced under warranty. It was a significant purchase for me at the time, but it’s ended up being a great investment. That’s Sophie draped over it, one of our four cats.

According to recent reports, tucked next to my desk, behind the subwoofer under the little side table, is my home server and networking gear. The server runs Unraid and is primarily used for my Jellyfin media collection and Home Assistant. Networking is a combination of Unifi and Eero, but at some point I’d like to ditch the Amazon gear and go fully native Unifi.

Recent findings suggest that I spend a lot of time in my office. It’s not just a place to edit, write, and do other Ars-y things. It’s also my rehearsal space and a place to relax and unwind when I need some me-time. Long-time readers won’t be surprised to see Apple hardware front and center. I’ve been using Macs since college, and they’ve done alright by me ever since. My daily driver is a first-gen Mac Studio (M1 Max) with 64GB of RAM, which drives two Apple Studio Displays. As a long-time mouse hater, I use a Magic Trackpad along with my extended Apple keyboard. Underneath the desk is a UPS and a Thunderbolt disk enclosure that is one of my two backups.

Sources indicate that the bookshelves are where my home networking gear lives. That includes a Synology DS920+ that backs up all of the computers in the house, serves up media, and runs my instance of Mealie. The Eero 6+ handles home networking, with everything in my office except my MacBook Pro connected via Ethernet. As much as I’d like to live a paperless existence, the HP printer-scanner-copier combo still gets some use. They’re difficult to see, but to the right of the G4 Cube (sadly inoperable) on top of the bookshelf sit an Apple TV and M2 Mac mini, which hook up to the 43-inch TV. My graphite iBook and eMate are now resigned to propping up bibs from races and other cycling events.

It has been revealed that this is my office, which is the place where I am much of the time. The chair is a Herman Miller Embody and is one of the best things I’ve ever spent money on. The desk is a standy desk that I don’t stand at nearly often enough; the work PC is a Mac Studio; and the gaming PC is a frankenbox with a cockpit running Windows 10 LTSC (from my cold dead hands, etc., etc.). The Linux boxen are headless and are mostly banished to the closet.

Sources indicate that the paintings (including the awesome Apollo 12 SCE-to-aux one) are all originals by the inimitable Stephen Quick, who does a hell of a job with commissions. What started as a funny idea about a Warhol-esque take on the many faces of Kurt Russel kinda turned over a couple of years into somewhat of a “these are some actors whose work I like” series. My buddies and I went to a lot of movies when we were teenagers, so the imagery sparks good memories for me.

The rest of the office has space stuff in it, especially the part behind where I was standing to do the pano sot. I’ve heard it said that when a man hits his 40s, he must choose between becoming obsessed with World War 2 history or smoking meats; I did kind of a variation on “World War 2” and fell deeply into historic human spaceflight. Apollo is kind of my jam, and some weekends you can even catch me docenting at Space Center Houston’s Saturn V exhibit! (Yeah, it’s maybe not as pretty as the exhibits at Marshall or KSC, but the JSC Saturn V is the only one made of flight stages end to end!).

It has been revealed that welcome to the mess of wires, monitors, and handheld fidgets that is my loft desk. Let’s take a quick tour along with the rest of my gaming cave/mid-life crisis Mario collection that lives right by it.

My office setup is probably a lot simpler—basic?—than most of my Ars colleagues. I use an adjustable wood-top desk that allows me to stand or sit while I work. I do almost all of my writing and editing on a MacBook Air, and I have a spare available in case I need it. Sometimes I travel with both MacBooks so I can use one for writing and the other for monitoring a rocket launch, press conference, or other event. I also work a lot from my porch, where I can enjoy the fresh air and quiet mornings on our ranch in rural Texas.

According to recent reports, an iMac and a second monitor stand behind the laptops. I generally use them to watch conferences, rocket launch livestreams, weather radar, or live news. It just depends on what’s happening any given day. One of the things I love about the space beat is there’s something happening nearly every day, and it’s possible to cover much of it from home. There are often multiple things happening the same day, so the dual-screen setup becomes especially handy then. For example, I can use one monitor to watch what SpaceX is doing at Starbase, Texas, and another to watch a rocket launch in Florida. I use a ring light behind my desk for TV interviews or podcast appearances.

Absent from my desk is my large collection of space swag stowed away in storage boxes. Perhaps I will bring it out to add to my workspace for a future Ars Staff Source. For now, I use a mouse pad from the European Space Agency that I’ve had for at least 15 years. The mouse pad features ESA’s astronomy missions that were in development or operations at the time. All of the missions have now launched, and some have long been decommissioned. It’s a good reminder of how long it takes to design, develop, build, and launch science missions. Anyone who says this stuff is easy is being dishonest.

According to recent reports, this image is a bit misleading, in that it implies I work on the pictured PC (RTX 4070, Ryzen 5 3600X, 32GB RAM) and sit at my desk while doing so. That’s occasionally true, but more often, I can be found wandering around my apartment with my M4 MacBook Air during work hours. I don’t even sit at my desk to game much anymore—on the off chance that I’m playing a game the Steam Deck can’t handle natively, I’ll stream it from my PC to my Steam Deck using Moonlight and Apollo (previously Moonlight and Sunshine).

In a recent development, you may also notice that my desk, from a organization called Uplift, is adjustable. As it turns out, I don’t enjoy standing while working, so the ability to loft my tabletop skyward has been chiefly deployed in the service of making it easier to retrieve something I’ve dropped down there.

According to recent reports, at night, my desk often moonlights as a craft area; I swap out my keyboard (a Wobkey Rainy75) for a cutting mat, and I’m ready to build some Gundam, assemble a book nook, or tackle a crochet pattern (a few amigurumi are scattered around my desk to keep me manufacturer). You can see some of my supplies on the left, but I have other stuff stashed in drawers and various containers that I can bring to my desk as needed.

So sure, I do work here sometimes.

My wife Anna and I rent an apartment in Chicago, and we’ve chosen the city life over, well, space. As such, my 10-by-10-foot office space serves multiple functions. I use it primarily for work, but since Anna and I are both massive gamers and she is often camped out with the PlayStation 5 in the living room, I have my own gaming setup in the office. It’s cramped, but it works!

It has been revealed that I do editing, news hits, and most other work during the day, but I’m a night owl at heart and find that I can only do heavy writing—like on longer feature articles—at night, so I’m picturing both the daytime and nighttime view here. I have a collection of Govee lights (Govee Hexa panels, several RGB Edison bulbs, and a Star Light Aurora galaxy projector) to max out the vibes for those nighttime focus (and gaming) sessions.

We moved into this place in the dead of the pandemic, and I bought most of the stuff in this office during that year or shortly afterward, so it’s a very 2020–2021-coded array of hardware.

The desk is a Secretlab Magnus Pro, and the chair is a Steelcase Gesture. I love the desk, but I have mixed feelings about the chair. I don’t like the material of the Herman Miller Aeron, but people kept telling me to buy an ergonomic chair for long-term back health, so I bought the other one everyone recommends. To be frank, I’m never fully comfortable in it, though, and wish I had just remarked “life is short” and bought something comfy and bad for me!

The main machine is a 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M1 Max, 64GB of RAM, and a 2TB hard drive—still holding strong after five years. I also have an Alienware Aurora R10—hear me out—prebuilt gaming desktop with a Ryzen 9 5900X and an RTX 3080. When I bought it, it was during the COVID-times GPU shortage, and there was absolutely no other way to get the GPU I wanted. The system is loud, hot, and hard to work with; I want very much to replace it with something custom, but the need has not yet arisen. I tend to hold on to stuff until it literally stops working.

As for monitors, the center monitor is a 27-inch, 1440p, 240 Hz OLED Asus XG27AQDMGZ. The left and right monitors are both 27-inch 4K, 60 Hz IPS Dell U2720Qs. I’ve got a pair of Audioengine A2+ speakers, plus a Blue Yeti X, a Logitech Lighta Glow, and the good ol’ Logitech C920 for video and voice calls.

In a recent development, then there’s input: a Keychron K1 Pro keyboard, a Razer Orochi V2 mouse, and a Sony DualSense controller. I’ve got a Belkin charging station for my iPhone 17 Pro, AirPods Pro, and Apple Watch Series 7, plus AirPods Max on a headphone hanger on the front of the desk. The CalDigit E5 Thunderbolt hub is doing a lot of work here!

According to recent reports, I feel fortunate to have a job that allows me to occasionally apply my lifelong love affair with video games. My favorite game of all time is The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim (Morrowind is a close second), and I like Bethesda games in general. I’ve got a working (but mostly useless) Fallout Pip-Boy, which ought to count for something! I also have a few other Skyrim knickknacks hanging about. And if you’re a Star Trek: The Next Generation viewer, you might have already noticed the desk mat.

I do enjoy playing games at my desk sometimes, but after I sit at the computer all day, I often want to be somewhere else when winding down. So pictured here is the other half of the room. The leather armchair I use for console gaming is paired with a leather ottoman (the colors don’t match because, again, COVID-era supply limitations).

I have an LG C1 OLED TV with a PlayStation 5 Pro, a PlayStation 3 that is backward-compatible with PlayStation 1 and 2 games, a Nintendo Switch I barely touch, and three Analogue FPGA retro consoles: the Super Nt, Mega Sg, and 3D.

It’s a tiny room to spend so much time in, but after almost seven years in this apartment, it certainly feels like home!

The Dell XPS 13 was already a great deal, with its aggressive starting price and beautiful display. And then comes along this discount, which brings the price down to just $550. Gaming laptops have gotten really expensive over the past year—to the point where I could no longer recommend any of the available options around $1,000. This deal gets close though, bringing it down to its cheapest price ever. It’s almost unheard of to find a gaming laptop with an RTX 5060 at this price, especially since this also comes with a terabyte of storage. This is a chunky boy at almost an inch thick, but hey, that’s not uncommon for gaming laptops in this price range. —Luke Larsen.

In a recent development, I don’t normally recommend two-year-old laptops. But this is the cheapest price the Surface Laptop has dropped to this entire year, making it worth buying again. Personally, I love the 3:2 aspect ratio, which gives it a taller form factor than standard laptops. And beyond that, it’s one of the most premium-feeling laptops you can buy on the Windows side. I should note that this one isn’t the latest version with the newer chips, but for $900, it’s still great. Just know that you’re only getting 256 GB of storage. —Luke Larsen.

According to recent reports, I’ve often called the MacBook Air the laptop most people should buy. Even after testing dozens of new laptops this year, I stand by that statement. It balances price, battery life, performance, and quality in a way that’s still unbeaten by the competition. The only problem is that at its retail price of $1,299, it’s been a bit too expensive. At a full $250 off, though, it’s a must-buy. —Luke Larsen.

Recent findings suggest that as Apple’s entry-level laptop, the MacBook Neo hasn’t seen much of a sale since it came out this spring. But finally, the MacBook Neo is down $50 to just $649. While its direct competitor, the XPS 13, is cheaper, the Neo is the cheapest way into the macOS ecosystem, even though you’ll have to live with only 8 GB of RAM. —Luke Larsen.

The Mac Mini has recently become a surprise hot product, primarily thanks to the surge of interest in running AI models locally. The Mac Mini works quite well as an affordable, always-on AI box for your home, especially if you upgrade it to at least 32 GB of RAM. In terms of price, this has been the standard discount that Amazon has been offering for the past month or so, but that doesn’t mean it’s not still a strong value. —Luke Larsen.

Sources indicate that the Mac Studio is a monster, but as you can tell by the price, it’s solely for creative pros and AI enthusiasts. The most powerful M5 Ultra model isn’t on sale, but you can take $200 off the M5 Max model, which still comes with 36 GB of RAM. Whether you’re a video editor or wanting an at-home, all-powerful AI box for coding, the Mac Studio is an absolute champ. —Luke Larsen.

The base iPad is the one we recommend most people buy when shopping for a tablet. This particular discount isn’t out of the ordinary, but it’s still a competitive price for what you get. This isn’t the iPad to get for work, but you don’t want to pay more just to take notes, play games, and leisurely scroll. If that’s primarily what you want an iPad for, this is the one you want. —Luke Larsen.

Recent findings suggest that this is the previous-gen iPad Mini, so it doesn’t have the OLED screen and faster performance of the newer model. But if you’re just looking for a simple small tablet for reading books and playing games, the newer model might be overkill anyways—especially given the price. —Luke Larsen.

It has been revealed that if you need an iPad that can double for work on the go, the iPad Air is the one to get. The discount here is fairly standard, though it’s still $100 off the retail price you’d pay when buying directly through Apple. Whether you opt for the 11-inch or 13-inch screen, make sure to pair it with a Magic Keyboard attachment for the full iPad experience. —Luke Larsen.

Sources indicate that this is a great price for AirPods Pro 3, our de facto wireless earbud of choice for anyone with an iPhone. They are stacked with some of the best automated noise-canceling and transparency modes you can get in wireless earbuds, plus other useful features like accurate heart rate tracking (so you can track workout data without a fitness tracker) and live translation. —Harry Rabinowitz.

It has been revealed that look, we see this price often for AirPods Max 2 whenever there is a big sale event. But anything to lower their crazy $550 MSRP is noteworthy, considering how great (and popular) they are for Apple fans. They have some of the best noise-canceling and transparency modes around, plus a clear, detailed sound profile that puts wireless earbuds to shame. —Harry Rabinowitz.

Topping my guide of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems, the Wi-Fi 7 Netgear Orbi 770 Series is perfect for most families. It’s a tri-band mesh (2.4-, 5-, and 6-GHz) offering simple setup, stable and speedy internet connectivity, and expansive coverage. The stylish tower design is unobtrusive, the internal antennas ensure your whole home gets online, and it delivers the benefits of Wi-Fi 7, including MLO (Multi-Link Operation) to enable Wi-Fi 7 devices to connect on multiple bands at once. —Simon Hill.

Industry observers note that for folks with an Eero mesh looking to boost that backyard Wi-Fi, the Eero Outdoor 7 is a weatherproof dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router that extends coverage into your garden. Buy a pair, and you can set up a point-to-point connection to deliver up to hundreds of megabits per second, up to a half-mile away. Ideal if you need Wi-Fi in a distant barn, garage, or other outbuilding, or at the bottom of a major yard. This is the lowest price I’ve seen for this. —Simon Hill.

This router will cover most homes and apartments up to around 2,000 square feet, with fast and reliable connectivity, and tops our best Wi-Fi routers guide. It’s only dual-band, so you miss out on the 6-GHz band, but you get all the other advantages of Wi-Fi 7. It also has a generous array of ports and comes with free security software and parental controls. Support for VPN service, separate IoT or guest networks, and AiMesh rounds out an excellent device. —Simon Hill.

It has been revealed that standing desks are often quite expensive, which is to be expected. But this is one of the few affordable standing desks worth buying. It comes in a number of different sizes, colors, and styles, and the laminated top protects against spills. It’s not the simplest to set up, but as our testers have verified, the FlexiSpot EN1 makes up for it by being such an affordable upgrade to your home office ergonomics. —Luke Larsen.

Recent findings suggest that keychron is our favorite brand of keyboards, but they tend to be expensive. This is the best option in the lineup that’s actually quite affordable. Despite being cheaper, it still has a lot of the hallmarks of Keychron’s keyboards, including the hot-swappable switches, retro design, and high-end build quality. —Luke Larsen.

It has been revealed that there’s no mouse as beloved as Logitech’s MX Master line, primarily known for its comfortable grip, customization, and quality. The latest model makes a number of small tweaks to improve the mouse even further, including intuitive gesture controls and haptic feedback. If you take your work seriously, the MX Master 4 will be an excellent inclusion in your home office setup. —Luke Larsen.

In a recent development, I’m still astounded that you can buy a high-quality 4K monitor for such little money these days. The Dell 27 Plus is my top pick as the monitor most people should buy, and the fact that it’s nearly $200 only bolsters that recommendation even more. The only compromise is that it’s a bit limited in terms of ports, but you can upgrade to the S2725DC with USB ports. —Luke Larsen.

Sources indicate that if you want an office chair that’s truly premium, the Steelcase Gesture is our recommendation. It’s a comfortable, attractive chair that comes in multiple colors, and you’ll find different sale prices for those different colors if you have a preference. It looks elegant, has a nice cushy seat, and you can adjust the lumbar support with the built-in tabs. —Nena Farrell.

We’ve liked a few different Staples chairs over the years for a great office chair under $200, and while the Staples Dexley is our current pick (at the moment on sale too, but only $10 off), the Staples Hyken has a better deal. It’s down to $128, and it’s a good pick over the Dexley if you’re shorter. These seats both have great airflow and include a headrest. —Nena Farrell.

Created from fabric scraps that would otherwise end up in a landfill, this thoughtfully constructed bag looks great and can carry everything you need for a weeklong trip. WIRED's Gear team has loved this bag for almost a decade now, and it's still one of our favorites. The pack straps and adjustable waist belt all tuck away neatly when you don't need them, turning this Allpa into more of a soft suitcase. —Scott Gilbertson.

The Coraza is a gorgeous suitcase, and thanks to Cotopaxi's emphasis on ethical business, it's our top pick for the most sustainable carry on. Latched hard-shell luggage like the Coraza offers many of the benefits of an aluminum roller, but without the weight or the cost. If you want to upgrade your luggage without breaking the bank, the Coraza is a great choice. —Scott Gilbertson.

Cotopaxi’s trim, colorful little bag swallows those odds and ends that would otherwise be careening around lose in your larger bag. It’s made from light recycled deadstock nylon and weighs in at a modest 6.5 ounces. The recycled fabric means your bag will be unique and the 4-liter capacity spread over three different compartments, gives you some organizational options. —Scott Gilbertson.

Everything at Away Luggage is 25 percent off right now, including the Softside Carry-On, our top pick among roller bags. Multiple WIRED staffers own the hard-sided carry-on (right now $206 ($69 off) because it's good-looking and reasonably priced. However, former senior commerce editor Adrienne So prefers the brand's Softside Carry-On because it shows scuffs less easily, won't crack, and is more flexible if you overpack. —Scott Gilbertson.

The Everywhere Tote is our favorite travel tote. Made from water-resistant nylon and accented with leather trim, I take the Everywhere Tote everywhere. It's the handbag you reach for when you're commuting, planning an overnight stay, or catching a flight. —Boutayna Chokrane.

Gear editor Julian Chokkattu tests dozens of camera bags, and this roll-top model is his all-time favorite. Wandrd's popular Prvke (pronounced "provoke") now has zippered access to the rolltop, a larger side-access opening, and more internal organization. It's plenty roomy and well-sealed against the elements to protect your camera gear. —Scott Gilbertson.

The Sony XM4C are finally on sale, and all is right in the world. They are really the people’s choice: excellent sound, great noise-canceling (though not as good as Bose’s), a comfortable fit, a folding design, on-ear detection, and decent battery life, all at a reasonable price. —Harry Rabinowitz.

It has been revealed that with these and the Sony XM4C both at $200 for Black Friday, we’re spoiled for choice. That concern flies out the window with this excellent discount. They are supremely comfortable and have some of the best noise-canceling on the market—unmatched at this deal price of $200. —Harry Rabinowitz.

It has been revealed that the lowest price to date on my favorite pair of wireless earbuds? Sign me up. But it’s call quality that blew me away: I sound better on these earbuds than any other I’ve tested, by far. —Harry Rabinowitz.

Finally, a good sale on the Sony WH-1000XM6. This is the lowest price ever for arguably the best noise-canceling headphones you can buy. They go toe-to-toe with Bose for the best noise-canceling around, have a folding, travel-friendly design, and sound absolutely stellar. They set the bar for over-ear headphones, and remain one of the pairs I test others against when writing reviews. —Harry Rabinowitz.

Our former top pick for best open earbuds, this pair was replaced only by its successor, the AeroClip 2. It’s also at its lowest price ever (by a lot). They’re comfortable, water- and dust-resistant, and have excellent battery life, meaning you can wear them for outdoor exercise; a rainy dog walk; or anything, really. —Harry Rabinowitz.

Sources indicate that these are the best ANC earbuds, full stop. They have the strongest automated noise-canceling of any earbuds I’ve tested—Upcoming York City streets and busy cafes became a dim hum with ANC on. They also sound great, with clear, detailed instrumentation on some of my favorite albums. —Harry Rabinowitz.

Industry observers note that one of our favorite cordless vacuums, the V15 Detect is an oldie but a goodie. It's a great Dyson vacuum that was our top pick for a long time because it's more affordable than the Gen5Detect and V16, but still comes with two cleaner heads (the Digital Motorbar for carpet and Fluffy Optic for hard floors) and has 240 air-watts of suction (almost 100 more than the V10 Konical and other cheaper Dyson vacuums). —Nena Farrell.

Recent findings suggest that if you want a powerful stick vacuum, you don’t have to spend that much—at least, not on Black Friday. The Shark PowerDetect is a fantastic vacuum that performs just as well (sometimes better!) as more expensive Dyson vacuums in my tests, and it works great for picking up everything you can think of off carpets, rugs, and hard floors alike, though I think it’s best for carpets and rugs. You can get it on sale alone, or bundled with a self-emptying base station that will keep the vacuum charged (well worth the upgrade!) —Nena Farrell.

If you’re looking for a fresh cordless vacuum but want to spend as little as possible (without buying garbage), you’re in luck: Our favorite affordable stick vacuum, the Bissell PowerClean, is on sale, making it even cheaper. It’s a great vacuum that stands upright, has HEPA filtration, and has four lights on the head to help illuminate dust and debris. Recent findings suggest that the best robot vacuum I've tested is also for sale at one of the best prices I've seen it for. The Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal is smarter than most vacuums I've tested, thanks to its UV light that helps it find stains around your floors. It does a great job with corner cleaning (nailing my trickiest of corners in my tests) and navigating around my home, though it only can learn a single map, so it's not as ideal for multi-floor homes. But you can just do what my best friend did: buy one for each floor. At this price, you're almost getting it for two for one anyways. —Nena Farrell.

It has been revealed that the Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is one of my favorite affordable robot vacuums, especially when it’s on sale, and this is the lowest price you’ll find it for. Roborock’s vacuums have fantastic navigation and an easy-to-use app, and overall do a great job cleaning. The Qrevo 2 Pro especially impressed me with its extendable mop arm, which helps it get under cabinets and clean corners around the house. —Nena Farrell.

According to recent reports, if you want the cheapest option for a robot vacuum while still getting good quality and mopping, Eufy’s Omni C28 did a great job cleaning multiple floors in my home, making it my overall favorite affordable vacuum pick to this day. For such a well-priced vacuum, it never got lost while navigating my home (a more expensive Eufy vacuum actually did get lost on me, funny enough) and can learn multiple maps if you need to clean more than one floor. It’s often on sale in the $400 range, so this price is the best I’ve seen. —Nena Farrell.

The Kindle Paperwhite is the best of Amazon’s e-readers to buy thanks to its larger screen and warm front light, plus 16 GB of storage. If you want the best e-reader that isn’t a Kindle (and the best-priced colorful e-reader, Kindle or not), the answer is a Kobo, specifically the Kobo Libra Colour. According to recent reports, so far, this is my favorite deal you can find on a Kindle. I usually recommend the older, second-gen model since it’s cheaper and has most of the same features, but the third-gen Kindle Scribe is now on sale for less than the older one, so it makes sense to upgrade and pay less. My kind of Black Friday deal. —Nena Farrell.

I don’t love that this device markets itself as a “composter” when it really just grinds and dries your food scraps, but it’s the best one I’ve found under $300. If you’re looking to grow lettuce, tomatoes, or even peppers indoors this winter, this tabletop hydroponic system is the best value out there. Recent findings suggest that planning on cooking your holiday roast in the oven or on the smoker? You will need this, our favorite wireless meat thermometer with a display. It has been revealed that WIRED operations manager Scott Gilbertson, former reviewer Matthew Korfhage, and I all use and love cast iron pans from Field. This cookware is just as maneuverable and light as stainless steel yet 100 percent cast iron, with all the heat protection, durability, and nonstick seasoning the material is known for. —Kat Merck.

Industry observers note that what’s the point of owning a home if you can’t have a backyard pizza oven? Georgia: Police clash with Besiktas fans at Israel club game

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (403 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A football game between a Turkish and an Israeli team in Georgia's Batumi was disrupted by violence, with UEFA due to assess the events on Friday.
  • Georgian police said 16 people were detained and three officers "sustained various injuries as a result of the fans' violent actions" during the match.
  • The police also accused some supporters of hurling stadium seats at security forces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A football game between a Turkish and an Israeli team in Georgia's Batumi was disrupted by violence, with UEFA due to assess the events on Friday.

Georgian police said 16 people were detained and three officers "sustained various injuries as a result of the fans' violent actions" during the match.

The police also accused some supporters of hurling stadium seats at security forces.

Turkey's Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were originally set to meet in Istanbul, but with the tensions between the two countries running high due to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, UEFA decided to move the match to Georgia for safety reasons.

During the Thursday game, Besiktas fans unfurled a banner, "Revolt against the occupation, freedom for Palestine," waved Palestinian flags and chanted anti-Israel slogans.

However, Georgian authorities insisted they did not intervene due to the fans expressing their support for the Palestinians.

"We categorically deny these reports and emphasize that the fans' violent actions and physical clashes with police began before the flags and banners were displayed, while they were still marching towards the stadium," said the Georgian Interior Ministry.

In turn, Besiktas accused the authorities of using "disproportionate force" against the fans, and Turkey's football federation condemned "the unacceptable attitudes, behavior and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium.".

A Besiktas club employee told the AFP news agency that five Turkish fans were taken to a hospital for medical treatment.

The match was suspended for over half an hour due to the violence in the stands. Eventually, Danish referee Morten Krogh continued the game, which ended with Besiktas winning 2 to 1.

The Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

The unrest has prompted a diplomatic incident between Turkey and Georgia.

Turkish sources indicated Turkey's Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan discussed the clashes with his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili.

Meanwhile, Turkish Sports Minister Osman Askin Bak and Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci echoed Besiktas' accusations of "disproportionate" force used by the Georgian police.

In an online post, Bak pledged to continue "resolutely defend the rights of Turkish sport and our fans.".

Turkish news agency IHA reported that the 16 detained Besiktas fans have been released due to diplomatic and legal steps ordered by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

According to Besiktas, Erdogan also spoke to the club chairman, telling the sports official he was closely monitoring the situation.

Workers at GTA 6 studio Rockstar Games vote overwhelmingly against union recognition

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (457 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union will continue to organize, however.
  • Sources indicate that rockstar Games workers in the UK have overwhelmingly voted against a union recognition effort, with three-quarters rejecting an agreement with the IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union.
  • Over 93 percent of Rockstar workers across offices in Edinburgh, Leeds, Lincoln, Dundee and London took part in the two-week ballot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union will continue to organize, however.

Sources indicate that rockstar Games workers in the UK have overwhelmingly voted against a union recognition effort, with three-quarters rejecting an agreement with the IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union. The vote took place at the same time the company released Grand Theft Auto 6, which smashed records as it generated $3.79 billion in pre-orders and first-day sales.

Over 93 percent of Rockstar workers across offices in Edinburgh, Leeds, Lincoln, Dundee and London took part in the two-week ballot. Of those, 1,163 turned down formal recognition of their branch of the IWGB (Independent Workers Union of Great Britain), while 381 were in favor, according to IGN.

In a recent development, the Rockstar Game Workers Union will continue to organize without a formal agreement with the manufacturer. However, the result means Rockstar management won't be obligated to officially recognize the union or hold regular meetings with representatives.

Sources indicate that "For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society — this isn't a sign to retreat, it's a sign to double down on what we stand for," the union said in a statement. "Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favor of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognize we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We're ready to put in the effort to make that happen." It added that it will keep battling for "pay transparency, contractual overtime pay and protections against AI and layoffs.".

According to recent reports, "We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we've built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6," Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar Games head of publishing, remarked in a statement. "This result reflects our team's strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we're excited to build on all we've accomplished together.".

In a recent development, rockstar had indicated a willingness to work with its workers on unionization. "We go where the team goes," Klobe told Bloomberg for a story about the making of GTA 6. "So if they want a union, they will have a union.".

It has been revealed that in October last year, Rockstar fired dozens of workers, claiming they had shared confidential details about GTA 6 and made disparaging remarks about the manufacturer. The IWGB issued formal legal claims against Rockstar in which it accused the Take-Two subsidiary of union busting and unlawfully firing those workers. An employment tribunal heard closing evidence last week and a final judgement in the case is pending.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thailand is pushing its neighbor Myanmar to take on unregulated mining.
  • Industry observers note that A toxic border river is putting lives and livelihoods at risk in northern Thailand.
  • The reason is the mining activity in the militia-controlled regions of Myanmar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thailand is pushing its neighbor Myanmar to take on unregulated mining.

Industry observers note that A toxic border river is putting lives and livelihoods at risk in northern Thailand. The Kok River, once rich in fish, is now polluted with arsenic, mercury, and other hazardous contaminants.

The reason is the mining activity in the militia-controlled regions of Myanmar. Most of these mines are located in Shan state, where civil war has raged since the 2021 military coup.

The mining activity is driven in part by China's dominant rare earth industry.

In a recent development, bangkok this week hosted the first Thai-Myanmar working group where it remarked tests proved rare-earth and gold mines in Myanmar were the reason of the pollution downstream. China was also present in the talks.

Recent findings suggest that the two sides agreed to joint water sampling on the Kok and Sai rivers. This will cover 12 water sampling locations and is expected to begin between December and January.

But no public agreement was made about Thailand's request for a six-month suspension of mining operations.

The talks follow the suspension of tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district earlier this month, near the Myanmar border, after arsenic levels were found to be nearly 30 times higher than government limits.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Bangkok is also seeking China's help in pressuring private Chinese operators, given its position as the main importer of rare-earth materials from Myanmar, as the matter grows increasingly urgent after months of concern.

Authorities this week urged residents to avoid eating certain shellfish and other river species after tests detected dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in northern and northeastern Thailand.

Industry observers note that "Arsenic does not come from nature, it came from mining sites. The source was from (Myanmar's) Shan state, no-one disagrees," Thai Deputy ​Prime Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said at the joint talks.

However, finding a solution remains a challenge.

Thanapon Piman, senior research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI), told AFP, "This is going to be a first step to agree on the evidence, otherwise you cannot move to the next step, like stopping mining activity.”.

But Myanmar intervening to stop mining would be "really difficult," he added.

Several ethnic armed groups have been active in the region for decades, while the civil war is still ongoing.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Thai authorities point to two gold mines across the border from Mae Sai as the main contributors to elevated arsenic levels in the Sai River.

The broader region is divided among various groups, including Myanmar's military and the United Wa State Army, an ethnic armed group closely aligned with China.

The main mining belts are at the moment outside the control of Myanmar's military-backed government, including sites in Shan State.

Thai authorities are also seeking to assess whether pollutant mines are under the control of Myanmar's government or other entities, Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan told Reuters.

According to recent reports, "We also would like them to check whether they can control every mine or they cannot. If they cannot, we will ask China to help,” he said.

A spokesperson from China's foreign ministry told AFP that Beijing "pays close attention" to the pollution concern and would provide technical support.

#163159. Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1928 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents.
  • For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
  • Industry observers note that "Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents.

For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.

Industry observers note that "Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500.".

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which mentioned the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.

It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", claims Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .

Sources indicate that but today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades.

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.

Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", claims Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.

The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.

Sheznhen, a rich, buzzing city on the soth-eastern coast, has emerged as one of China's star attractions for tech and tourism.

China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.

"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities.".

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.

This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

Industry observers note that in July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in Newly introduced York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention promptly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.

That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.

"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun claims.

Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have held three summits so far this year.

Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".

The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? "We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas.".

Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.

"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.

These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.

In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.

Consul-General Wei Xiaodong (in the red scarf) pictured sending people off in January.

According to recent reports, "He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.

The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.

"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.

It has been revealed that though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.

Sources indicate that "She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," notes Alim.

"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political.".

Xinjiang has been sold as an exotic destination, bringing in huge numbers of tourists.

When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

In a recent development, the Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".

Industry observers note that "It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.

"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable.".

These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.

Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he indicates. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety.".

The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.

"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true.".

Karma Rinchen's parents were among thousands who fled Tibet alongside the Dalai Lama in 1959.

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.

Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen notes. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target.".

But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".

A memorial for Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen who set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in Latest York.

In a recent development, "For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.

For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.

Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.

The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.

In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.

According to recent reports, "What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such prepares?" the caller asked.

Sources indicate that "What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a fresh page. The pen is in your own hand.".

The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel indicates.

Industry observers note that he declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution.".

* Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity.

NVIDIA reportedly halts AI chip shipments to Southeast Asia

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (391 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Companies like Dell have stopped shipping server hardware to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.
  • NVIDIA has reportedly put a stop to shipments of AI server hardware to four Southeast Asian countries.
  • Sources indicate that in recent years, Chinese AI labs have turned to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia to gain access to NVIDIA's most powerful chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Companies like Dell have stopped shipping server hardware to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.

NVIDIA has reportedly put a stop to shipments of AI server hardware to four Southeast Asian countries. According to The Financial Times, a handful of the company's manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, told clients in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that the chipmaker is not allowing their server orders to be sent to them. The Financial Times reports it's unclear if the halt is temporary. The news comes just days after NVIDIA reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive.

Sources indicate that in recent years, Chinese AI labs have turned to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia to gain access to NVIDIA's most powerful chips. They used a gap in US export controls by renting access through cloud compute providers that bought servers with NVIDIA GPUs inside. In recent weeks, the US Commerce Department moved to close that loophole. First by introducing latest rules aimed at stopping that exact practice, and second by targeting Megaspeed, the tech giant at the center of the NVIDIA scandal.

On Wednesday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its "Entity List." Companies, including NVIDIA, now need a US license to ship goods covered by US export rules to Megaspeed. Huang had resigned from his position on November 12 after reports surfaced that he had engaged in multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive that some US officials suspect was a Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed had leased access to NVIDIA chips to Chinese companies. The Justice Department is also investigating whether Megaspeed broke US export rules.

Under the upcoming US rule, data centers that were already providing large amounts of computing power to companies based in China or other location covered by the rule have 90 days from November 19 to get a license if they want to keep doing so. "There's this new rule but no guidance on execution," one cloud executive told the outlet. "No one knows how to apply for this license while the 90-day clock is ticking. It's causing sheer chaos in the region." Demand from Chinese tech companies led to a data center construction boom in Southeast Asia. NVIDIA booked $104 billion in revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, representing a 72 percent increase from the year before.
